<summary>Text description of this diagram</summary>

**The stack, in the order the guidance recommends completing it**, and who owns each part.

| | Document | What it holds | Owns it |
|-----|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| 1 | Analytical plan | The question, the purpose, why the decision matters, the commissioner, the dates | Team |
| 2 | Scope | The decisions it supports, inputs and outputs, boundaries and limitations, resources, principal risks | Analyst |
| 3 | Assurance level decision sheet | Whether it meets the requirements of Business Critical analysis. Saved and attached to the Specification | Commissioner and Analyst |
| 4 | Specification | Calculations, assumptions, expected accuracy, and the testing that shows it meets its purpose | Analyst |
| 5 | Quality assurance plan | The register of assurance actions: owner, priority, progress, target date, tied to appraisal reference codes | Analyst |
| 6 | QA appraisal, basic information | Model name, identifier and contact, and the four named owners | Analyst |
| 7 | The analysis or model itself | No template, because models differ. The Model Guidance Document instead. Fills the data, assumptions and risk registers | Analyst |
| 8 | Technical guide | Enough for someone with no prior knowledge to take over its operation and development | Analyst |
| 9 | User guide | Enough for a new team member to run it and produce the expected outputs | Analyst |
| 10 | QA appraisal, assurance review | Six worksheets scored, with a reason for each rating and the actions it raises | Critical friend, as Lead Assurer |
| 11 | Quality assurance sign-off | The Assurance Report worksheet: what was reviewed, the statement, the risks, and the approval | Critical friend, then the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer |

**The four owners every Business Critical analysis names**, and they are the playbook's four
roles. The **Analysis Senior Responsible Officer** signs the approval statement that the model is
fit for purpose and approved for use. The **critical friend**, who on Business Critical work is
the **Lead Assurer**, owns the assurance review and the review statement. The **analyst** owns the
scope, the specification, the model and both guides. The **commissioner** knows what the analysis
is for and what depends on it. They are recorded on the Named Owners worksheet at step 6.

**One workbook, three stages.** The quality assurance appraisal is twelve worksheets, completed at three points in the life of
the analysis rather than in one sitting. Basic information at step 6, as soon as the model has a
name. The analysis or model review, while the model is built and tested. The assurance review at
step 10, by the Lead Assurer with the analyst.

**The assurance review scores six areas**: documentation, governance and oversight, structure and
clarity, data and assumptions, verification, and validation. Outputs is a seventh that NHSBSA has
still to define. Every requirement carries a reference code, so a quality assurance plan action can
be traced back to the criterion that raised it: the Scope document is D1. Actions are prioritised
**Must**, essential to address a significant risk, issue or control weakness; **Should**,
recommended to improve quality, robustness or assurance; or **Could**, additional benefit but not
needed for an acceptable level.

**Sign-off is not the end of it.** Quality assurance continues after an analysis is judged fit for purpose. It is used as intended,
with its caveats. Errors are logged and improvements recorded. Data and assumptions are kept
current through scheduled reviews. Any
material change triggers a review of the documentation and of the assurance requirements,
proportionate to the change, and the scope, specification, both guides, the appraisal and the
quality assurance plan are all in scope of that review.

**Where the stack lives, and what it is called.** All analytical documentation is held centrally by
the Quality and Assurance Team, which is the authoritative source and maintains the NHSBSA register
of analytical models. Analysts may keep working copies locally, but each new production version of
the model goes to the team as it is released. Name every file type first and analysis second, so
the stack can be recognised at a glance: Scope_Specification_AnalysisName, User_Guide_AnalysisName.

Quality assurance is rarely linear. A review that raises a question about the method sends you back
to the technical guide, the specification or the scope, and that is the process working rather than
failing.
